- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes in history (e.g., 85+), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “rebound” or “mean reversion” effect.
- Model underestimates when true price drops below 75, especially if recent history shows volatility or downward momentum.
- Model overestimates when history includes a recent high followed by a sharp decline — fails to adjust downward quickly enough.
- Model shows persistent bias toward higher prices in the first 10–15 days of forecast, suggesting lag in adjusting to recent downward trends.
- Model fails to capture “mean reversion” toward historical average (e.g., 75–80 range) after sustained spikes or drops — tends to hold onto extremes longer than reality.
- When true price drops below 70, model often fails to recognize the trend and continues to forecast higher — suggests underweighting of recent low prices.
- Model tends to “smooth” volatility — underestimates sharp drops and overestimates gradual declines — especially in the last 5–10 days of forecast.
